name: Adam Rex
bio:
Adam Rex received a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the University of Arizona. He got his start drawing comic strips for the Arizona Daily Wildcat student newspaper and making art for games such as Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering. His Magic work began with the Mirage expansion in 1996, while he was an undergraduate in the illustration department. He has illustrated many cards across a large number of sets.

Outside Magic, his role-playing game work includes Planescape books for TSR and Changeling: The Dreaming. He has also contributed illustrations to periodicals including Amazing Stories, Cricket and Spider. He received the Jack Gaughan Award for Best Emerging Artist in 2005. He went on to become the author and illustrator of dozens of children’s books, including the New York Times bestselling Frankenstein Makes a Sandwich and Chu’s Day, written by Neil Gaiman. His debut novel, The True Meaning of Smekday, was shortlisted for the Andre Norton Award for Young Adult Science Fiction and Fantasy. His awards include the Margaret Wise Brown Prize in Children’s Literature and the National Cartoonists Society Book Illustration Award. Although he went on to focus on children’s books, he still occasionally makes art for games such as Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering.

His style often features soft, expressive brushwork, blended transitions, warm earthy colours, and dramatic contrasts between light and shadow.

name: Carl Critchlow
bio:
Carl Critchlow is a British fantasy and science fiction illustrator, best known for creating Thrud the Barbarian, which first appeared in White Dwarf magazine. He began working for Games Workshop in the early 1980s while still at art college, and went on to work for 2000 AD, DC Comics and Wizards of the Coast. He has also illustrated the Wheel of Time Roleplaying Game and Star Wars supplements.

He debuted in Magic with Weatherlight in 1997 and has illustrated numerous cards across many sets. His Magic work often features animals and creatures such as rats, goats, cats, hounds, bears, elephants and wurms.

His painting style is instantly recognizable, with a grungy, textured look that leans toward the grotesque and violent, which suits his dragons and monsters for Magic cards.

name: Christopher Moeller
bio:
Christopher Moeller was born in Ithaca, New York. He earned a BFA in painting from the University of Michigan School of Art and an MFA in illustration from Syracuse University. His professional debut was in 1991, writing and painting Innovation Comics’ Rocketman: King of the Rocketmen, and in 1994 he moved to Dark Horse Comics. He specializes in fully painted graphic novels. His signature creation is the Iron Empires science-fiction universe. He is also known for DC work, including covers for Lucifer and the painted graphic novel JLA: A League of One.

His first Magic card appeared in Urza’s Saga in 1998, and his first illustration was Expunge. He has illustrated 260 Magic cards across 168 sets. He has also painted cards for the World of Warcraft TCG, covers for White Wolf’s Aberrant and packaging art for Axis & Allies Miniatures.

Bold brushwork and strong silhouettes are trademarks of his style. Painting comics and card art takes a knack for painting things simply and legibly, largely from imagination.

name: Daniel Ljunggren
bio:
Daniel Ljunggren is a concept artist, illustrator and 3D artist based in Stockholm, Sweden. He has worked for studios including DICE, Cellar Door Games and Unique Development Studios. His game credits include illustration on Just Cause 2 (2010), art on theHunter (2009) and art director on Generation Zero (2019). His first Magic card appeared in Worldwake in 2010.

His style is modern and versatile.

name: Jesper Ejsing
bio:
Jesper Ejsing was born in Copenhagen, Denmark. He discovered fantasy through the works of Tolkien and was introduced to Dungeons & Dragons on Christmas Day in 1986. In 1993, while studying Danish literature at a local university, he saw Magic for the first time at an RPG convention in Odense. He soon realized that illustration was his true calling. He began his career as a colorist in comic books, then moved on to book covers and Magic: The Gathering, and later worked as a concept artist in the gaming industry.

He has been creating Magic art since Lorwyn in 2007. He is responsible for a large number of cards, tokens, schemes and planes, and has been part of numerous design teams that shaped the visual identity of Magic’s worlds.

His brand of dark but colorful whimsy has been a staple of the game since he started. He is particularly known for dragons and dragon-like creatures.

name: Mark Poole
bio:
Born in Goldsboro, North Carolina, Mark Poole graduated from the University of South Carolina in 1986 with a BFA in fine arts and design. He works mostly in acrylic, oil and digital media.

He began working on Magic: The Gathering in 1992, a year before the game launched, as one of about 25 artists Richard Garfield brought in for the first set. His early Magic art is bold and playful, with bright, saturated characters set against detailed landscapes, made to read at a glance on a small card. His later oil paintings are more precise and dream-like, with textured surfaces and an atmospheric, imaginative-realist feel.

He has also worked for companies such as White Wolf Publishing, Warcraft, Sony Online Entertainment, Upper Deck and Ziggurat Games.

name: Quinton Hoover
bio:
Quinton B. Hoover was born in Fruita, Colorado, and died in Oklahoma City at the age of 49. He started out as a comic artist. Early on he was already a skilled sketch artist, and working with another artist taught him brush, watercolor and acrylics.

He was one of the original 25 Magic artists. He illustrated Magic cards until 2008, with 1993 to 1999 being his prime. In all, he illustrated 71 Magic cards across 54 sets. In the 1990s he also made card art for Iron Crown Enterprises’ Middle-earth Collectible Card Game.

His style is often described as strong lines with a stained-glass quality, and it helped make many early cards vivid and memorable. One tribute says his comic-art roots made his style markedly different from the other early artists’. One reviewer singles out his careful rendering of drapery and clothing detail. In his later years he tried to adapt his style to what Magic’s art directors wanted, but it didn’t work, and his Time Spiral and Lorwyn cards are hard to recognize as the work of the same artist.

name: Randy "rk" Post
bio:
Randy “rk” Post was raised on a farm in Illinois. He took illustration classes at Northern Illinois University with Mark Nelson before turning to fantasy illustration for games. He did freelance work for TSR, then became a full-time staff illustrator there in September 1996, painting covers for games and novels. After Wizards of the Coast bought TSR, he moved to Wizards’ northwest offices. He has contributed art to Magic since Exodus, and his best-known Magic pieces include Morphling. He later moved into 2D and 3D art for video games alongside his freelance Magic illustrations. His other clients have ranged from Nintendo to Marvel.

His art has been described as having Gothic stylings. He names no specific artist as an inspiration, and his style has been shaped by many genres. One reviewer has called him a cornerstone of RPG art around the turn of the millennium.

name: Svetlin Velinov
bio:
Svetlin Velinov was born in Varna, Bulgaria. He trained at the “Dobri Hristov” National School of Arts and works as a freelance concept artist and illustrator. His clients include Wizards of the Coast, Hasbro, Sony, Creative Assembly, Capcom, Games Workshop, Blizzard Entertainment and Applibot. His game credits include card art for Artifact and Artifact: Foundry, illustrations for Pathfinder Adventures, and additional illustrations for Duels of the Planeswalkers 2012 and 2013.

He began illustrating for Magic with Worldwake and is one of the game’s most prolific artists.

His illustrations and paintings feature beautifully realized characters and creatures, and his fantasy work has appeared in the Legend of the Cryptids series for Applibot. He creates both fantasy and sci-fi themed work.

name: Thomas M. Baxa
bio:
Thomas M. Baxa debuted in Magic: The Gathering with Tempest in 1997. Since then he has illustrated numerous cards across tens of sets, mostly dark fantasy creatures.

Baxa grew up in the suburbs of Chicago and studied at Northern Illinois University under the comic and fantasy artist Mark Nelson. In 1989 he started creating interior illustrations for Dungeons & Dragons books and Dragon magazine.

His work has a creepy and often disturbing edge that appeals to fantasy and horror fans alike, with a focus on dynamic action and innovative character design.

name: Vincent Proce
bio:
Vincent Proce was born and raised in Chicago, where he lived and raised his son, and he has worked in almost every field of 2D art. He started in graphic art, then moved into comics (Comico), 2D animation (Warner Bros., Animaniacs, Histeria), video games (including Mortal Kombat and Stranglehold), tabletop games (D&D and Magic) and movies (Pacific Rim: Uprising). At Midway Games he was a concept artist, and on Mortal Kombat vs. DC Universe he painted the ending art and worked in the cinematic department.

His first Magic job was the Zendikar concept art push. He used his vacation time from another job to work in Seattle with Mark Tedin, Richard Whitters, Matt Cavotta and Jeremy Jarvis.

His work has a gritty, rusty quality, which he says comes from the rusty, gritty background of his life. He says his versions of Magic characters are often a bit too twisted to make it into a set. His Scythe Specter hides details such as tortured souls burning behind the rib cage of its flying mount, and he lists it, along with his Eldrazi designs for Zendikar, among his favorite monsters.
